data.title: StraitsX, OCBC and Standard Chartered complete tokenised deposit payment test
data.description:
US dollar payments can now be settled within minutes and outside conventional banking hours.

StraitsX, OCBC and Standard Chartered have completed a test using tokenised deposits issued by different banks for payments between financial institutions, settling US dollar payments within minutes outside conventional banking hours.

The proof of concept, carried out under the Monetary Authority of Singapore’s BLOOM initiative, addresses a growing challenge as banks build their own tokenised deposit ecosystems.

Because tokenised deposits are claims only against the bank that issues them, they cannot be moved easily between different banks’ ecosystems, which may run on different platforms and standards.

The test used StraitsX’s shared settlement infrastructure to coordinate payments across OCBC’s and Standard Chartered’s tokenised deposit ecosystems, covering payment initiation, compliance screening, liquidity checks, settlement and confirmation. Tokenised deposits from both banks were treated as equivalent within the shared framework.

“Tokenised deposits have the potential to enable near-instant and programmable money movement, but their broader utility will depend on how effectively different banking ecosystems can connect,” said Tianwei Liu, CEO and co-founder of StraitsX.

Many traditional interbank US dollar payments run within fixed settlement windows and are unavailable outside business hours. In the test, payments settled outside conventional cut-off times, with compliance, liquidity and settlement processes completed within minutes.

The participants also found the shared model reduced the need for bilateral prefunding between institutions, pointing to more efficient liquidity management than conventional models.

Broader rollout will require further work on legal, regulatory, operational and commercial arrangements, including settlement finality, liquidity management, participant responsibilities and financial crime controls.

Any commercial implementation remains subject to regulatory engagement, participant approvals, legal documentation and operational risk assessments.

data.title: Banks plan own digital money but industry leaders question the odds
data.description:
JP Morgan and Ripple doubt bank consortia can scale tokenised deposits.

Banks are choosing tokenised deposits over stablecoins, but industry leaders are questioning whether bank consortia can deliver them at scale.

Speaking at a panel discussion at the Singapore FinTech Festival on 19 November, Umar Farooq, global co-head of payments at J.P. Morgan, said banks are forming groups because stablecoins pull liquidity out of the banking system.  

Farooq pointed to a 21-bank group on the dollar side, a European consortium, and Project Agora, which involves central banks.

“Such groups are building closed systems, which is a good first step but not a feasible end solution”, he said. Banks would eventually need to accept each other’s tokenised assets, he added.

Brad Garlinghouse, chief executive of Ripple, was blunter, calling the bank consortia ‘almost dead on arrival '. He said this opens room for fast-moving, nimble players.  

Ralph Hamers, chairman of Banking Circle, said trust is the basis of any such arrangement. “Everything happens only because there is trust,” he said.

On the stablecoin side, Farooq said the market stood at around $300b on 1 January and is at the same level today. “If this thing were explosive, you would see the stock go up through the roof,” he added.

Hamers cited McKinsey figures showing stablecoin volume has doubled in two years but accounts for only 0.02% of all money moving globally. Garlinghouse read the same figure as headroom. “That’s all opportunity,” he said.

Farooq said J.P. Morgan’s Kinexys platform processes more than $2 trillion in business-to-business transactions annually, which he described as much bigger than stablecoin volumes in that segment.

Use cases include weekend foreign exchange settlement for payment service providers in Asia, which avoids pre-funding, and margin payments for oil and gas companies when US markets are closed.

Meagen Burnett, chief financial officer at Schroders, said the asset manager will not issue a stablecoin, offer payments, or tokenise deposits.

“Because stablecoins pay no yield, Schroders instead launched a tokenised money market fund with J.P. Morgan through the Central Bank of Ireland, with corporate treasury as the next target,” she added.

Richard Teng, co-CEO of Binance, said traditional and crypto players are increasingly collaborating, citing DBS’s announcement a day earlier that it is working with Circle.

Hamers said he expects consolidation amongst the growing number of rails and currencies.  

Farooq added that faster rails also raise the stakes if trading becomes automated. “There are no new problems—there are always old problems that are augmented because of new technology,” he said, adding that circuit breakers would be needed if agentic trading grows.

He also warned that markets will eventually face a discontinuity, as in 2022, with quite negative outcomes if everything is automated, tokenised and running around the clock.

data.title: Standard Chartered rolls out tokenised deposits in Singapore
data.description:
This builds on its launch of tokenised deposit services in Hong Kong.

Standard Chartered has launched its tokenised deposits solution in Singapore, built on its proprietary blockchain infrastructure,

This is expected to enable near real-time transactions across Singapore and Hong Kong, the bank said on 19 November 2026.

Eligible clients can utilised their commercial bank deposits within digital treasury and investment workflows, including intragroup liquidity management, Standard Chartered said.

The solution supports multiple currencies including SGD, HKD, USD, EUR, CNH, GBP.

Standard Chartered rolled out tokenised deposits in Hong Kong on 2 November.

Companies that have made live tokenised deposit transactions include China AMC, Finloop, and PantherTrade, Standard Chartered Hong Kong said. It is also working with Fireblocks and Hashkey to expand the reach of its tokenised deposit solution.

Earlier in 2026, Standard Chartered bought Zodia Custody, a digital asset custody business.

data.title: Mastercard and Ant test AI agent business payments in Singapore
data.description:
It aims to verify AI agents' identity and permissions for consumer and business transactions.

Mastercard and Ant International have completed a Singapore pilot that tested how businesses can securely authorise AI agents to purchase digital services within predefined spending limits, as the companies also demonstrated a live consumer AI payment in Asia Pacific.

The two completed an Agent Pay for Machines (AP4M) pilot with Antom in Singapore, testing how businesses can allow AI agents to make purchases whilst maintaining control over spending limits and approved activities.

The pilot allowed an AI agent to use credentials, policy controls and payment authorisation features to purchase digital services within parameters set by the business.

Meanwhile, the companies conducted a live consumer transaction through Antom, Ant International’s merchant payment and digitalisation platform, where an AI agent purchased a cup of coffee based on a consumer’s pre-approved intent.

The transaction used Mastercard Agent Pay with Verifiable Intent, which creates a record of what the consumer authorised the AI agent to do.

The technology combines network tokenisation, authentication and consumer intent verification to support agent-initiated payments.

The move comes as AI agents become more involved in commerce. Mastercard said establishing trust around identity and authority will be critical to wider adoption.

“AI agents are already capable of completing payments. The bigger challenge now is creating the trust for consumers, businesses and merchants to embrace them,” said Joyce Bo, executive vice president, Core Payments, Asia Pacific, Mastercard.

The companies said the collaboration aims to help merchants accept purchases from AI agents acting within consumer- or business-approved permissions, whilst enabling new AI-driven commerce models.

“Trust creates a foundation for merchants to rethink how they deliver value, from reaching more customers through AI agents to offering services in smaller, flexible units that agents can discover, combine and purchase,” said Chunmao Zhu, vice president, Technology & Business, Antom.

The developments come as companies explore how AI agents could move beyond assisting users to directly carrying out tasks such as shopping, payments and business procurement.

data.title: Visa and Alipay+ expand QR payment access for Singapore travellers
data.description:
Users can pay at Alipay+ merchants with linked Visa cards.

Visa has rolled out its Scan to Pay service with Alipay+, allowing eligible Visa cardholders to pay at participating QR merchants across Asia Pacific, including Singapore.

The service allows travellers to use their Visa credentials through participating digital wallets to scan and pay at Alipay+ merchants without downloading a separate local payment application.

Under the arrangement, Google Wallet users from supported markets can use eligible Visa cards to scan and pay at participating Alipay+ merchants when travelling to Singapore.

Samsung Wallet users in Singapore and Australia can also use eligible Visa cards to pay at participating Alipay+ merchants in Hong Kong and Malaysia.

The service is enabled by Visa Pay, which supports interoperable QR payments through digital wallets and banking applications.

It allows participating wallet providers to extend the international acceptance of Visa credentials whilst retaining their existing customer-facing applications.

Visa said it plans to expand the rollout to more wallet users and destination markets as the partnership develops.

data.title: AI payment agents promise B2B gains but raise accountability concerns
data.description:
Visa, SMBC and Temasek flag the need for stronger transaction controls. 

Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are opening up new opportunities in business payments and corporate treasury, but questions over transaction authority, cybersecurity, and accountability could complicate wider adoption, executives said.

Speaking at a panel discussion during the Singapore FinTech Festival on 19 November, Stephen Karpin, president for Asia Pacific at Visa, said AI-driven payments are beginning to gain commercial traction, particularly in business-to-business (B2B) transactions.

He said rules-based B2B payments and money transfers are amongst the earliest applications being automated, whilst machine-to-machine transactions and smaller payments could create further opportunities.

However, Karpin noted that wider adoption would require systems that can verify AI agents, restrict their transaction permissions, and determine responsibility when payments go wrong.

“When something goes wrong, we need to be able to confirm exactly what the instructions were,” he added.

For instance, Karpin said Visa has developed its Intelligent Commerce credential for agentic payments, using tokenised payment credentials and passkeys to authenticate users and limit what AI agents can purchase.

“Once an agent receives it, there are specific parameters covering the user's intent, limitations and controls,” he added.

Karpin said restrictions could include maximum transaction amounts and merchant types, whilst transaction records could help determine whether errors originated with buyers, sellers or AI agents.

Akio Isowa, senior managing executive officer and group chief digital innovation officer at SMBC, identified corporate treasury and cross-border payments as potential applications for the technology.

Isowa said programmable deposits could allow businesses to transfer funds based on predefined conditions, manage liquidity more dynamically and reduce delays in cross-border settlements.

“When combined with AI, these capabilities could eventually help companies anticipate liquidity needs and execute appropriate financial actions more efficiently,” he added.

Isowa also identified opportunities in delivery-versus-payment settlement, which links asset transfers with corresponding payments to reduce settlement risks and improve capital efficiency.

However, customers must be able to specify what an AI agent can do, how much money it can transfer and under what conditions. “Banks would also need strong authentication, transaction monitoring, and mechanisms to stop or escalate activity when something falls outside those permissions.”

“The important distinction is between allowing AI to make recommendations and giving it authority to move money,” Isowa added.

Meanwhile, Pradyumna Agrawal, managing director for investment at Temasek, said autonomous financial transactions could create new business models, building on existing digital infrastructure and automation.

However, he warned that the technology could introduce risks that existing financial regulations may not fully address.

“Authentication is not the problem here. It's a question of authorisation. It's a question of completely new legal frameworks on who is actually accountable for these things,” Agrawal said.

He also warned that large numbers of AI agents operating simultaneously could exploit longstanding cybersecurity vulnerabilities at a greater scale.

Beyond the risks, Agrawal said banks could explore new revenue streams by offering services beyond traditional banking products, including storing data credentials and distributing financial products from other companies.

data.title: IMF’s Katz says AI question is earnings not whether bubble bursts
data.description:
AI companies are not the same as the Dot-com era firms, as the AI firms have earnings growth.

The question of whether the artificial intelligence (AI) bubble is not whether it will burst, but whether earnings can be sustained.

“I think the real question is what will the real economy effects be if it turns out that the technological promise of AI is not what investors may be expecting, and when and and is not what has been showing up in earnings to date,” said Dan Katz, first deputy managing director at the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

Unlike the Dot-com era of the late 1990s and early 2000s, where companies with no revenue were valued based on clicks, the company valuations in the AI space look reasonable as they showcase earnings growth, Katz said in a speaking session during Day 2 of Singapore Fintech Festival 2026 held at the Singapore EXPO, 19 November.

The question now is if the AI companies can sustain their revenue and earnings, Katz said.

“I would say that I think we need to be open-minded to scenarios where AI-related investments have a lower rate of return associated with than those that are associated with expectations today and also be open-minded that AI-related investments may be even more profitable than some people are underwriting today,” Katz told Sopnendu Mohanty, Group CEO of GFTN, who moderated the session.

Mohanty had pointed out that the revenue promised by the AI economy is not matching the timing of assets actually delivering value.

“There’s [also] high replacement cost, because technology is rapidly changing, by the time it generates revenue, the next technology comes in,” Mohanty said.

Katz said that the IMF is “watching very closely” how financial market correction may ripple out through the credit markets.

“I think we're also seeing evidence that maybe some of our expectations around how quickly value in the chip ecosystem, for example, are going to depreciate, are not maybe as rapid as we thought,” Katz said.

“What we're advising our member countries is to think through a range of scenarios because there is just so much uncertainty around how this revolution is going to play out,” Katz added.

Katz and Mohanty also discussed stablecoins, with Katz recognizing both its potential for financial inclusion and improving payment systems, but also the unique risks that it brings.

Katz said that it is too early to tell whether stablecoins can serve as an alternative rail for cross-border settlements, especially for low-income and middle-income countries.

He said that the most important benefit about regulatory developments on stablecoins is that it had pushed the rest of the financial system to rewire their businesses to deliver some of the promises associated with stablecoins.

data.title: MAS explores AI agent protocol and tokenisation framework
data.description:
MAS is setting up a sandbox to test AI agents and programmable money for corporate treasury and payments.

The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) will further explore artificial intelligence (AI) agents and tokenisation, setting out plans for a new agent verification protocol, a new sandbox, and updated tokenisation guides.

Whilst adoption of AI agents are still in the early stages, it has the potential to scale rapidly as the industry realizes that it can cut costs and ramp up speed of search and comparison, optimisation and decisions, negotiations and execution, said Chia Der Jiun, managing director of MAS, said in his keynote speech for Day 2 of the Singapore Fintech Festival (SFF) on 19 November.

Chia identified AI agents and tokenisation as the two transformative forces in finance.

“We do not know how quickly agentic transactions will grow, but it is likely that the future will be a mix of the human economy and a new agent economy,” Chia said.

MAS said that it will work to develop a common protocol to verify agents’ representation and mandate, as well as a sandbox to explore AI agents and programmable money, Chia said.

“The two initiatives I've highlighted, common protocols for agent transactions and the sandbox for agentic money, will be important building blocks for the future of agentic transactions,” Chia said.

The common Know-Your-Agent protocol will require customers and financial institutions to exchange information about the agent’s identity, representation, authority, mandate it operates under, and provenance.

MAS believes that this will give financial institutions the information needed to determine the terms and the scope of permission that the agents hold, Chia said.

MAS is also setting up a sandbox with the Future of Finance Institute, bringing together AI agents and programmable money for corporate treasury management and payments services, he said.

Chia recognized that AI can sharply reduce information asymmetries, reduce search and information costs in economic decisions, and enable more dynamic and continuous pricing.

For businesses, agents can automate procurement, inventory management, and other routine commercial decisions, he said.

Tokenised collateral and digital money
Chia said that MAS will work with the industry to onboard and tokenise other commonly used collateral, including foreign government securities and money market funds.

Chia announced the launch of the Guardian Tokenised Collateral Framework, which sets out the operational requirements across the collateral life cycle, including eligibility, custody, valuation, return, and enforcement.

“We are updating the guide on tokenisation of capital markets products to further clarify the regulatory and risk management requirements,” Chia said, adding that they are also working with local legal professionals to clarify issues relating to the tokenization of capital markets products.

These efforts build on MAS’ earlier issue of $100m in tokenised bills, announced by Chia during the 2025 edition of SFF.
https://sbr.com.sg/news/singapore-trial-tokenised-mas-bills-using-central-bank-digital-currency

Chia also outlined various initiatives and new frameworks in Singapore relating to tokenisation, stablecoins, and central bank digital currencies (CBDCs), including the rebranding of SGD Test Net to the SG Ledger, a settlement platform for tokenised assets, forms of digital money, and ledgers.

MAS also released the Bloom Field Guide on 19 November, which details practical considerations for deploying digital money in various cases.

Chia said that MAS tested mechanisms to settle and verify settlement conditions across separate central bank systems with the Bank of England, the Bank of Thailand, and Deutsche Bundesbank.

“This is our approach: collaborate with the industry to lay the foundations and prepare the building blocks, so that the industry can scale where there are commercially compelling use cases,” Chia said.

Chia sees the future of finance as an interoperable ecosystem involving AI agents, financial institutions, and digital money.

“Businesses, financial institutions, financial infrastructure operators will have to adapt to serving both human customers and agents,” he said.

Chia said that financial institutions will have to strengthen their value proposition, and potentially consider whether limits are needed on agent-instructed transactions to manage risk.

Regulators will have to consider the implication for financial stability as agentic use in financial markets and money movements expand.

“Importantly, consumers and businesses need to retain meaningful control over the objectives, mandate, and actions of their agents. Autonomy has to be bounded,” Chia said.

data.title: Fraud rate drops 36% but attacks grow more complex: study
data.description:
Deepfake fraud fell 37%, the second-largest drop in Asia-Pacific after China.

Singapore’s fraud rate dropped 36% year on year (YoY) to 1%, according to a Sumsub study released on 18 November.

Deepfake fraud also fell 37% YoY, the second-largest decline in the Asia-Pacific (APAC) region, behind only China at 59%.

However, Sumsub said attacks are growing more complex. Singapore’s fraud complexity index (FCI) rose 9% to 2.13 points, above the 2.09 APAC average.

APAC topped the six regions in the report, accounting for 33% of fraud networks and close to a million confirmed fraud attempts globally.

Sumsub said regulators in Singapore are shifting responsibility for scam payments and mule accounts to institutions that send, receive or facilitate these transactions, and are building new ways to share fraud intelligence.

Singapore recently rolled out several laws against fraud, including the Protection from Scams Act and the Scams (Countermeasures) and Other Matters Act 2026. A National Scams List was also released to support information exchange on suspicious scam accounts.

Sumsub said APAC businesses suffer from external fraud (42%), followed by scam-induced payments (40%). Amongst consumers, 79% experienced fraud in the past 12 months, with half of victims losing money and 51% recovering none.

data.title: UOB explores A*STAR's multilingual AI for client calls
data.description:
It can interpret questions and concerns across different languages and accents.

UOB is exploring the use of an artificial intelligence (AI)-powered multilingual customer call solution to enhance customer engagement across ASEAN languages and markets.

The bank said it looks to apply the solution, powered by A*STAR's Multimodal Empathetic Reasoning and Learning in One Network (MERaLiON) model, to help relationship managers (RMs) understand, engage, and advise customers in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Vietnam.

The first phase will be done through Project AURA, the bank’s strategic programme to deploy advanced AI at scale and build an AI-fluent culture.

The solution, called the Compliance Intelligence Engine and Evidence-Grounded Post-Call Compliance Review System, can support relationship managers during customer conversations by interpreting questions and concerns across different languages, accents, and communication styles.

It can provide relevant prompts on considerations such as key product information and risk disclosures to complement relationship managers’ professional judgement and help them deliver clearer and more relevant customer conversations.

After each conversation, the solution can support an evidence-grounded review to assess whether key information was communicated clearly and fair dealing standards were met, providing an additional layer of governance for the bank.

It could also improve productivity by reducing manual translation and automating parts of the post-call review process, whilst providing insights for more targeted relationship manager coaching.

Relationship managers would remain accountable for the conversations and advice they provide, with AI complementing their professional judgement.

“Banking is built on trust, and every customer conversation matters,” said Leong Yung Chee, group chief financial officer at UOB.

“We want to apply AI with purpose, and we see potential for this solution to help our RMs better understand customers, navigate language and cultural nuances, and provide clearer, more relevant guidance,” Leong added.

MERaLiON supports multilingual processing and code-switching across 11 ASEAN languages, including Malay, Bahasa Indonesia, Thai, and Vietnamese, alongside English, Mandarin, Singlish, and traditional dialects such as Cantonese.

The model has achieved the lowest average word-error rate among open-source models across seven languages, according to UOB and A*STAR.

UOB said it will continue to assess how the model's capabilities can be applied safely and responsibly across its regional franchise.
